note: Circles for PSLE: the formulas, the parts, the pi decision, and the four strategies for odd shapes, cutouts and shaded regions.

formulas.title: The four you must have without thinking

rows.note: r is the RADIUS. If you are given the diameter, halve it first.

rows.formula: 2 x pi x r, or pi x d
rows.note: Use pi x d when the diameter is given; it saves a step and a mistake.
The single commonest slip in the whole topic is using d where r belongs.
Needed constantly in composite figures where a diameter is a straight edge.

pi.title: Which value of pi to use
pi.rule: The question usually tells you. If it gives you a choice, let the numbers decide.

decide.when: The radius or diameter is a multiple of 7: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49.
decide.why: The 7 in the denominator cancels with the number, leaving whole numbers and no decimals to round.

decide.when: The radius or diameter is not a multiple of 7, especially 5, 10, 20, 50, 100.
decide.why: Multiplying by 3.14 is easy on these, and 22/7 would give an ugly fraction.

pi.warn: If the question states a value, use exactly that one even if the other looks easier. Using the other value changes the answer and loses the mark.

parts.title: Parts of a circle, and the perimeter trap
parts.intro: Area is easy: take the fraction of the whole circle. Perimeter is where marks are lost, because the straight edges count too.

rows.watch: No straight edges. The whole boundary is curved.

rows.area: half of pi x r x r
rows.perimeter: pi x r, PLUS the diameter (2r)
rows.watch: The flat edge is part of the boundary. Forgetting the diameter is the commonest perimeter error in PSLE.

rows.area: a quarter of pi x r x r
rows.perimeter: half of pi x r, PLUS two radii (2r)
rows.watch: Two straight edges, both of length r. Many students add only one.

rows.area: three quarters of pi x r x r
rows.perimeter: three quarters of 2 x pi x r, PLUS two radii
rows.watch: Same two straight edges as a quadrant, because the cut is the same shape.

parts.goldenRule: For PERIMETER, trace the outline with your finger. Every piece your finger travels along counts, curved or straight. Every line inside the shape that your finger never touches does NOT count.

strategies.title: Four strategies for odd shapes
strategies.intro: Almost every hard circle question is one of these four. Decide which one you are looking at before calculating anything.

list.name: Subtract the cut-out
list.when: A smaller shape has been removed from a larger one, leaving a hole or a ring.
clue: shaded region is what is left
a circle cut from a square
how: Find the area of the whole outer shape as if nothing were removed.
Find the area of the shape that was removed.
Subtract the second from the first.
list.worked: A circle of radius 7 cm is cut from a square of side 14 cm. Outer square = 14 x 14 = 196. Circle = 22/7 x 7 x 7 = 154. Shaded = 196 - 154 = 42 square cm.
list.trap: For the PERIMETER of a shape with a hole, the hole's edge counts too, because your finger travels around it. For AREA you subtract; for perimeter you often add.

list.name: Cut and paste
list.when: The shaded pieces look scattered and awkward, but could be slid together into a simple shape.
clue: two identical leaf or petal shapes
the figure is made of quadrants of equal radius
how: Look for a shaded piece that is exactly the same shape and size as an empty piece.
Slide the shaded piece into the empty one, in your head or with a light pencil arrow.
Keep going until the shaded region becomes a square, rectangle, triangle or half a circle.
Then use the ordinary formula on that simple shape.
list.worked: A rectangle is 10 cm by 6 cm. A semicircle of diameter 6 cm is added on the right edge, and an identical semicircle of diameter 6 cm is cut out of the left edge. The piece added is exactly the same shape and size as the piece removed, so it fills the gap perfectly. The area is just the rectangle: 10 x 6 = 60 square cm, with no need to work out pi at all.
list.trap: Only slide pieces that are genuinely identical, meaning the same shape AND the same size. Roughly similar is not enough. Also note that the PERIMETER here is not the rectangle's perimeter, because two straight edges have been replaced by two arcs.

list.name: Split into known pieces
list.when: The figure is clearly built from circles, semicircles, quadrants, rectangles and triangles stuck together.
clue: a shape made of several arcs
how: Draw light lines to cut the figure into pieces you have a formula for.
Work out each piece separately and write each answer down as you go.
Add the pieces for area. For perimeter, add only the outside edges.
list.worked: A running track is a rectangle 20 m by 14 m with a semicircle of diameter 14 m on each end. Area = 20 x 14 plus two half-circles of radius 7, which together make one whole circle: 280 + 154 = 434 square m.
list.trap: The cutting lines you drew are inside the figure. They do not belong to the perimeter, and a common error is to include them.

list.name: Handle the overlap
list.when: Two shapes cross, and the region where they cross is counted twice if you simply add.
clue: a lens or leaf shape between two arcs
how: Add the two shapes as if they did not overlap.
Notice the overlapping middle has now been counted twice.
Subtract the overlap once to correct it.
list.worked: Two circles of radius 7 cm overlap. Together they cover 250 square cm of the table. Each circle is 22/7 x 7 x 7 = 154, so separately they total 308. But the table only shows 250 covered, so the overlapping middle has been counted twice: 308 - 250 = 58 square cm is the overlap.
list.trap: Decide first which region you want: the overlap itself, the parts outside it, or everything covered. Naming it before calculating stops you adding and subtracting the wrong pieces. Note also that two quadrants drawn in a square do not always cover the whole square, so never assume the union is the square.

routine.title: How to attack a circles question

steps.do: Write down r and d for every circle in the figure before anything else.
steps.why: Half of all errors are a diameter used as a radius. Writing both kills the error at the start.

steps.do: Decide: is the question asking for AREA or PERIMETER? Circle the word.
steps.why: They need different methods and the words look similar when you are rushing.

steps.do: Choose your pi from the numbers: multiple of 7 means 22/7, otherwise 3.14, unless told.
steps.why: The right choice removes decimals and rounding entirely.

steps.do: Name the strategy: subtract, cut and paste, split, or overlap.
steps.why: Naming it first stops you from calculating things you will not use.

steps.do: If perimeter, trace the outline with a finger and list every edge you travel along.
steps.why: This is the only reliable way to avoid adding inside lines or missing a diameter.

steps.do: Keep each piece on its own line with a label, then combine at the end.
steps.why: Method marks are awarded for the pieces even when the final total is wrong.

steps.do: Check the units: square units for area, plain units for perimeter.
steps.why: A correct number with the wrong unit is not a correct answer.

traps.fix: Write r = and d = at the top for every circle before starting.
traps.cost: Area comes out four times too big.

traps.trap: Forgetting the diameter on a semicircle perimeter
traps.fix: Trace the outline with your finger. The flat edge is part of the journey.
traps.cost: The commonest perimeter error at PSLE.

traps.trap: Adding only one radius on a quadrant perimeter
traps.fix: A quadrant has TWO straight edges, both of length r.
traps.cost: Short by one radius every time.

traps.trap: Counting internal cutting lines in the perimeter
traps.fix: Perimeter is the outside only. Lines you drew to split the shape are not on the boundary.
Choose once, at the top, and use it everywhere.
traps.cost: Inconsistent answers that cannot be checked.

traps.fix: Keep fractions or full decimals until the very last line, then round once.
traps.cost: Answer off by a small amount and marked wrong.

traps.trap: Assuming a shape is a semicircle because it looks like one
traps.fix: Check that the flat edge really passes through the centre. A shape cut off centre is not a semicircle.

traps.trap: Giving area units for a perimeter
traps.fix: Perimeter is a length, so cm or m. Area is cm squared or m squared.
traps.cost: One mark, every time it happens.

traps.trap: Not spotting that two radii are equal
traps.fix: In figures built from a square, arcs drawn from corners usually share the same radius, which is the side of the square.
traps.cost: You think there is not enough information when there is.

quickChecks: Is my area answer bigger than the shape could possibly be? A shaded part can never be larger than the whole figure.
A quadrant of radius r drawn inside a square of side r covers about 79 percent of that square. If your quadrant comes out bigger than the square, or tiny, check whether you used r or d.
If the radius doubled, area should be four times bigger, not two. Use this to sanity-check a big jump.
Perimeter answers should be in the same rough range as the straight dimensions given. A perimeter ten times the width of the figure is a sign an inside line was counted.

fractions.title: Arcs that are not halves or quarters
fractions.intro: A quadrant is a quarter and a semicircle is a half because 90 and 180 are quarters and halves of 360. Any other angle works exactly the same way, using the angle over 360.
fractions.rule: Fraction of the circle = the angle at the centre divided by 360. Use that same fraction for the area and for the arc length.
fractions.warn: The straight edges never scale with the fraction. A sector always has exactly two radii on its boundary, whatever the angle, and a semicircle has one diameter. Multiply only the curved part by the fraction.

worked.title: Worked all the way through
worked.intro: Every number here has been checked. Notice how often the perimeter needs a straight edge that the area calculation never touched.

list.q: A quadrant has radius 7 cm. Find its perimeter. Take pi as 22/7.
steps: Two straight edges, each a radius: 2 × 7 = 14 cm
list.note: The two radii are the part everybody forgets. Trace the outline with a finger and you cannot miss them.

list.q: A semicircle has radius 7 cm. Find its perimeter. Take pi as 22/7.
steps: The flat edge is a diameter: 2 × 7 = 14 cm
list.note: One diameter, not two radii drawn separately. It is the same length either way, but saying diameter keeps you from doubling it twice.

list.q: A three-quarter circle has radius 14 cm. Find its area and perimeter. Take pi as 22/7.
list.note: A three-quarter circle has the same two straight edges as a quadrant, because the cut is the same shape.

list.q: A running track is a rectangle 20 m by 14 m with a semicircle on each short end. Find its area and its perimeter. Take pi as 22/7.
steps: The two semicircles have diameter 14, so radius 7, and together they make one whole circle.
Perimeter = the two long sides + one whole circumference = 2 × 20 + 22/7 × 14 = 40 + 44 = 84 m
list.note: The two 14 m ends are NOT on the perimeter. Your finger never travels along them, because the semicircles are there instead.

list.q: A quadrant of radius 14 cm is cut from a square of side 14 cm. Find the shaded area left. Take pi as 22/7.
list.note: The quadrant's radius is the whole side of the square, not half of it. Read the diagram twice on this one.

list.q: A sector has a centre angle of 60 degrees and radius 6 cm. Find its area and perimeter. Take pi as 3.14.
list.note: Radius 6 is not a multiple of 7, so 3.14 is the sensible pi here, and the question says so anyway.

list.q: A ring is made by cutting a circle of radius 6 cm from a circle of radius 10 cm. Find its area and the total length of its boundary. Take pi as 3.14.
steps: The boundary is BOTH circles: 2 × 3.14 × 10 + 2 × 3.14 × 6 = 62.8 + 37.68 = 100.48 cm
list.note: For area you subtract. For the boundary you add, because your finger has to travel round the hole as well as round the outside.
